school.title:
Quiet at school.
Curious everywhere.
school.subtitle: The classroom saw one version of me
school.lead: My notebooks were unfinished, my handwriting untidy, and asking a teacher felt impossible. I still usually finished near the top of my class. Around people I knew, a different child appeared—one with questions about everything.

brother.title:
Someone who
kept answering.
brother.subtitle: Curiosity takes root
brother.lead: On the rooftop, I would ask, “Bhaiya, tell me something new.” He told me about stars, galaxies, black holes and time. With a brick, a pebble or a stone in his hand, he could turn an ordinary moment into a question I had never thought to ask.

english.title:
A cartoon became
a reason to learn.
english.subtitle: Listening. Imitating. Trying again.
english.lead: Phones could hold films, cartoons and whole other worlds. My brother patiently downloaded Doraemon over a slow connection. Later, Ben 10 gave me a reason to learn English: I wanted to understand the episodes I could not find in Hindi. A. J. Hoge’s listening lessons gave me a way to try.
english.aside: During those childhood years, I lost my father.

first-code.title:
Three hours.
Two numbers.
first-code.subtitle: July 2017 · our first program
first-code.lead: Faz helped over a voice call while my brother and I typed a program that added two numbers. Missing semicolons, misplaced brackets, another error. Three hours later, it worked. We began learning C together; when my brother stopped, I kept going.

fundamentals.title:
One instruction
at a time.
fundamentals.subtitle: Learning to follow the logic
fundamentals.lead: Variables, loops, patterns. Small programs helped me understand what each instruction did. A screen full of code was slowly becoming something I could follow.

experiments.title:
Then the lines
started moving.
experiments.subtitle: Code → shape → moving car
experiments.lead: I wanted to make games. First I learned to draw with code: circles, cars, an aircraft, a character. The red car was nothing like the one I imagined—but it moved. Each experiment gave me something new to show my brother.

beats.title: Learning to draw
beats.text: A circle, an error, another attempt. Repeated instructions were beginning to produce visible shapes.

beats.title: The moving car
beats.text: I could show my brother the red car—and explain the code that made it move.

beats.title: The idea and the attempt
beats.text: A detailed reference beside the simpler car I could draw. There was still a distance between imagining something and making it.

beats.title: An aircraft, drawn from lines
beats.text: On 29 October 2017, I was using the same drawing ideas to build an aircraft.

beats.title: A character on the screen
beats.text: By 7 November, those lines had become a character too.

beats.title: Could the computer make music?
beats.text: On 31 October, I began experimenting with sound functions and the notes behind a simple piano.

beats.title: A new editor. Another struggle.
beats.text: Code::Blocks felt like an upgrade from Turbo C. I also kept the photograph of a whole day spent trying to run one simple program.

first-web.title:
A browser became
my canvas.
first-web.subtitle: Notepad · HTML · CSS
first-web.lead: In November 2017, I was writing HTML in Notepad. Forms, logos and the Code Playground gave me another way to turn instructions into something visible.

blender.title:
I wanted to make
the videos, too.
blender.subtitle: From watching to making
blender.lead: Faz suggested Blender. At first it felt impossibly complicated; watching MJO gave me a reason to return. I built scenes, made animated films and taught programming and animation on my channel: Animation / Programming Guru.

laptop.title:
A tool
of my own.
laptop.subtitle: 20 January 2018
laptop.lead: The early programs were made on my brother’s laptop. Then I got my own. The unboxing, the specifications I saved, the winter evenings studying under a blanket—they are all still here.

beginner.title:
Online, I was
“Beginner”.
beginner.subtitle: A community that knew me
beginner.lead: SoloLearn made learning social: lessons, challenges, languages and people to compete with. One screenshot records my number-one India ranking for that month. Behind the profile was still the quiet child from school.
beginner.recollection: I remember a previous Platinum run taking three days. With a new account called Beginner, I tried to beat it. As I remember it, I reached Platinum in a day and a half—and was banned because my progress was suspected of cheating.

beats.title: Number one in India that month
beats.text: The saved profile records the monthly ranking. The Platinum time and ban are my recollection, separate from what this screenshot establishes.

beats.title: The first challenges
beats.text: C++ questions, early badges and small programs. I kept finding another thing to learn.

beats.title: The child behind the profile
beats.text: Photographs from that period and a project celebrating a hundred followers capture the life around Beginner.

typing.title:
Practice became
1.510 seconds.
typing.subtitle: A to Z · February 2018
typing.lead: I practised typing with all ten fingers, then began racing through the alphabet. The result screenshot survived: A to Z in 1.510 seconds. I remember being second on the world leaderboard that day.

css.title:
Try. Adjust.
Try again.
css.subtitle: Five attempts at a rainbow
css.lead: CSS let me build things I could see: a phone, shapes, logos, a rainbow loader. Even getting “Loading” into the centre became a story. I kept the attempts, including the file I finally named “Finally center loading with rainbow”.

games.title:
Something I made.
Something I could play.
games.subtitle: Unity · C# · learning by building
games.lead: I played my own Flappy Bird game on a phone and made a small forest shooter with a boar chasing the player. A harder idea—cars learning to race against a human—went unfinished. The mathematics was beyond what I knew, but trying taught me how training worked.
games.aside: The games are no longer in my archive. This diagram illustrates the learning path; it is not a game capture.

bus.title:
A first client.
A reason to deliver.
bus.subtitle: Around October 2020
bus.lead: My brother helped me find 3D work on Upwork. Our first bus-conversion model took roughly two months and paid $100. The client returned for a rooftop cabin; we earned $180 in total. The saved tour records something I finished for someone else.

web.title:
This time,
I chose a direction.
web.subtitle: Learning the web professionally
web.lead: Hearing about Faz’s website commission encouraged me to keep learning. I returned to HTML and CSS, responsive layouts and Frontend Mentor. Around the turn of 2021–2022, I did my first paid web work for EazyGrad, then continued into JavaScript and React.

work.title:
Building for people.
Helping people build.
work.subtitle: Harigurus → ProCodrr
work.lead: At Harigurus, I worked on a service for booking purohits for weddings and other ceremonies. When operations paused, I moved into social media management and helping develop courses for Anurag Singh’s ProCodrr channel. I spent about three years on that side of learning.

beats.title: Helping develop the courses
beats.text: Working through a course project, with real learners on the other side of the screen.

beats.title: Helping with questions
beats.text: I think about the child who could not ask a teacher. Helping someone work through a doubt feels especially meaningful from here.

today.title:
Different tools.
The same curiosity.
today.subtitle: From Turbo C to Octoverse
today.lead: On 24 October 2026, I bought a Claude subscription and began working on Octoverse, my more complex universe project. Looking from Turbo C and Notepad to the tools I use now makes the distance feel real. I am still finding things I want to understand.

beats.title: The traces I left behind
beats.text: Finding my old GitHub profile brought another part of the journey back into view.

beats.title: The next universe
beats.text: The start of working with Claude on Octoverse, in October 2026.
